Applicants should refer to applicable regulations and guidance(s) 38 for more information on what is required or recommended to be submitted to FDA in 39 applications for such products. 8
candidates.context: This guidance applies broadly to drug delivery devices. As appropriate, applicable consensus 32 standards and other guidance(s) may be referenced in conjunction with this guidance. 33 This guidance revises the draft guidance titled Essential Drug Delivery Outputs for Devices 42 Intended to Deliver Drugs and Biological Products that issued in June 2024. The guidance is 43 updated to clarify content on testing and controlling device drug-delivery performance and to 44 align with the revised 21 CFR part 820 Quality Management System Regulation (QMSR). 9

candidates.statement: EDDCs are based on product type (e.g., syringe, autoinjector, infusion pump) and product 137 specifics. These characteristics warrant design verification, design validation, control, and 138 maintenance, as appropriate, to demonstrate the drug delivery function performs as intended (i.e., 139 delivery of the intended drug dose to the intended delivery site) throughout the product 140 lifecycle. 26 Generally, EDDCs have specifications, including acceptance criteria that must be 141 met to ensure that the product performs as intended. These specifications with acceptance 142 criteria are generally included in the submission. 27 EDDCs are high-level characteristics that 143 incorporate lower-level characteristics or product features. If the specification(s) for an EDDC is 144 met, it should reflect that the specification(s) for the lower-level characteristic(s) related to that 145 EDDC are also met. For EDDCs, the lower-level characteristics or product features alone do not 146 ensure the intended drug delivery, and these data are generally not included in the submission for 147 purposes of ensuring the EDDC performance. 28 In addition, although the design considers the 148 user needs, the EDDCs are dependent on the functional design of the device (device design) and 149 not on the user actions. The following illustrates what an EDDC is and is not. 150
candidates.context: This section provides further description of EDDCs and a product-specific example of what is 133 and is not an EDDC. The appendices in this guidance provide examples of potential EDDCs for 134 different product types. 25 • What is an EDDC? It is a drug delivery aspect that: 152 o Is a high-level (i.e., system level) function that incorporates lower-level (i.e., 153 component level) aspects, and 154 o Depends on the functional device design. 155

candidates.statement: During the product’s lifecycle, the product can be exposed to multiple stressors prior to each use 234 that may influence performance of the device drug-delivery function. Preconditioning is a 235 method to simulate exposing the product to stressors prior to testing to which the product will 236 likely be exposed (including worst case scenarios) during storage, shipping, and before each use 237 (e.g., cleaning, reprocessing, storage (see section V.A.1.a), or repeat use, as applicable). 238 Applicants should identify preconditions applicable to the specific product, and verification 239 testing should assess the ability of the product to withstand those stressors. Applicants should 240 identify preconditions based on the risk of the product design, research and development 241 characterization testing, intended use, how the product will move from the manufacturer of the 242

candidates.statement: Preconditions to simulate storage include, for example, specific temperatures, temperature 254 fluctuations, pressure changes, and humidity. A product may be subjected to different storage 255 conditions throughout the product lifecycle (e.g., conditions at the manufacturing facility, 256 warehouse, health care facility, pharmacy, or home setting), and these should all be considered 257 before verification testing. 258

Preconditions to simulate shipping include, for example, vibration, shock, and pressure changes 262 that may impact device drug-delivery performance. Some EDDCs (e.g., physical dimensions) 263 would not be impacted by shipping and would not warrant preconditioning for shipping 264 conditions. For the EDDCs that may be influenced by shipping conditions, shipping 265 preconditioning representative of likely exposures (e.g., during shipping via air, ground by truck, 266 ground by rail, boat) should occur before verification testing. 267

candidates.statement: Overall, the design and development verification assessment of EDDC specifications should 303 occur after appropriate preconditioning. Depending on the product, the EDDC, and the specific 304 types of preconditions, there may be different types of testing to demonstrate that an EDDC 305 specification is met throughout the range of conditions and use environments described in the 306 proposed labeling. This testing can include functional testing after preconditioning or it can be 307 part of a design and development verification shelf-life testing program (see section V.A.2.b). 308 For example, an applicant could follow a protocol for assessing the impact of shipping 309 preconditions on a specific EDDC. candidates.statement: Sampling plans for design and development verification testing should be risk-based, taking into 322 consideration the indication for use, patient population, drug being delivered, context of use 323 (e.g., immediate or emergency use versus chronic therapy, home versus clinical setting), and 324 complexity of design and manufacturing. For example, a product with a higher risk profile 325 would warrant a more robust sampling plan than a product with a lower risk profile. Sampling 326 recommendations in recognized consensus standards could be used in developing sampling 327 plans, as appropriate, based on product-specific risk considerations. A design verification testing 328 protocol should include a statistical sampling plan. The plan should include justification for the 329 number of lots to be tested, taking into consideration the potential impact of lot-to-lot variability, 330 and acceptance criteria. The tested lots should be the final finished product. 331

For devices for which the intended use requires that the medical device 370 be connected to or interface with other medical devices, validation must confirm that the 371 requirements are met when connected/interfaced. 44 The most appropriate validation method may 372 depend on the application type, stage of development, product, and EDDC. 45

VI. CONTROL STRATEGIES FOR EDDCS 430

candidates.statement: The control strategy should be based on product and process understanding in combination with 440 risk management activities. 49 Product and process understanding can be drawn from sources 441 such as development of the device design and manufacturing process, structural analysis, design 442 and development verification testing, and prior knowledge from manufacture of similar devices. 443 Risk assessments can include consideration of factors such as the intended user (e.g., healthcare 444 provider, patient) and the context of use as well as the complexity of the EDDC (e.g., 445 interdependencies at the component level) and the complexity and robustness of the 446 manufacturing process. The result of the risk assessment is used to determine the need for risk 447 controls; this information is further used to inform the type and extent of controls appropriate for 448 each EDDC. The amount of information regarding the control strategy to include in an 449 application should similarly be commensurate with the risks and associated impact. 450
candidates.context: A control strategy is used to ensure that each lot of the final finished product is manufactured to 432 consistently meet its EDDC specification. For a given EDDC, an appropriate control strategy 433 might consist of one or more types of control steps at different stages of the manufacturing 434 process. Some control steps are performed earlier in the manufacturing process (e.g., upstream 435 controls such as in-process controls, control of process parameters, control of incoming 436 materials, and purchasing information). Other control steps are performed at the end of the 437 manufacturing process (e.g., a downstream control such as lot release testing). 438 Appropriate controls should be identified for each EDDC, considering the relevant features and 452 manufacturing process steps, and the documentation used to support these controls should be 453 identified. candidates.statement: Appropriate controls should be identified for each EDDC, considering the relevant features and 452 manufacturing process steps, and the documentation used to support these controls should be 453 identified. The control strategy can consist of one or more controls, implemented upstream, 454 downstream, or both, as previously stated. When developing an upstream control strategy for an 455 EDDC, it is important to consider the subsequent manufacturing process steps that can influence 456 the EDDC and provide a justification describing why the proposed upstream control is adequate 457 to ensure that the EDDC of the final finished product will meet its specification (i.e., after these 458 process steps occur). For certain EDDCs, purchasing information or an incoming 459 test/examination to confirm that the incoming product meets required specifications may be 460 sufficient (e.g., for the length of a syringe and needle that cannot change over the expiration 461 dating period). For other EDDCs, a singular downstream control (e.g., release testing) or a 462 combination of upstream and downstream controls may be appropriate. 463

candidates.statement: The data provided in IND 52 and IDE applications for drug delivery devices should reflect the 493 development stage of the product. It is understood that for combination products, the drug 494 delivery device could be introduced after the investigational drug development begins. We 495 understand that the device design may evolve based on study results. The device drug-delivery 496 data submitted in an IND or IDE application 53 should reflect the development process, and 497 applicants should consider the device design, the drug being delivered, the patient population(s), 498 study design, and risks to the study participants when determining the data to provide. 499 To support the first use of the device or device constituent part in a clinical study, it is important 500 that applicants provide information demonstrating that the safety and performance of the device 501 is adequate for the proposed investigation. Information from EDDC testing is provided to 502 demonstrate that the device performs and the drug is delivered (dose and delivery site) as 503 intended. 504
